Family Health

Haemorrhoid procedures: choosing an option and planning recovery

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A haemorrhoid procedure can help persistent symptoms, but the right choice depends on the diagnosis, the internal and external findings, and your priorities. Understanding the trade-offs and planning recovery are as important as knowing the procedure’s name.

Start with a diagnosis, not a procedure name

Haemorrhoidal tissue is a normal part of the anal canal. Problems arise when these vascular cushions enlarge, bleed, protrude or become painful. Internal haemorrhoids are inside the anal canal; external haemorrhoids are covered by sensitive skin around the opening. Someone can have both, and their treatments differ.

A clinician asks about bleeding, pain, bowel habits, prolapse and previous treatment, then examines the area. A small viewing instrument called an anoscope may help show internal tissue. Other investigations depend on the findings and history. Blood from the rectum should not automatically be labelled piles, because other bowel and anal conditions can cause it. Persistent bleeding after treatment also needs reassessment.

Most people do not need an operation

Measures that reduce straining and improve stool consistency are usually the starting point. Fibre, adequate fluids, suitable activity and avoiding long periods on the toilet may ease symptoms. Medicines or a stool-softening plan can be considered when appropriate. These measures remain useful even if a procedure is eventually needed.

Only a minority of people assessed for symptomatic haemorrhoids require surgery. Treatment may be appropriate for persistent bleeding, troublesome prolapse, large external disease or symptoms that have not improved with simpler care. Infection is not a prerequisite for treatment. Conversely, simply finding haemorrhoids does not mean an operation is necessary when they are not causing problems.

What the four grades describe

The grades describe prolapse of internal haemorrhoids. Grade I tissue remains inside. Grade II comes out, often during a bowel movement, but returns by itself. Grade III does not return without being gently pushed back. Grade IV remains outside and cannot be reduced.

This classification helps discussion, but it is not a pain scale or a grading system for every external lump. Severe pain may have another cause, such as a clot or fissure. Do not force painful protruding tissue back. The choice of treatment also depends on bleeding, external disease, general health, previous procedures and what matters most to you about recovery and recurrence.

Rubber-band ligation

Banding treats internal haemorrhoids by placing a small elastic band around tissue above the most pain-sensitive area. The band interrupts its blood supply; the treated part separates and the resulting scar helps fix the tissue in place. It is often an option for grades I and II and selected grade III haemorrhoids after conservative care has not been enough.

It is usually an office or outpatient procedure without a general anaesthetic. Pressure, aching or discomfort can occur; it should not be presented as guaranteed painless. Tell the clinician immediately about severe pain. More than one treatment may be needed, with timing chosen by the clinic rather than an automatic two-month interval. Only a trained clinician should perform banding. It is never a home treatment.

Injection sclerotherapy

Sclerotherapy involves injecting a substance into internal haemorrhoidal tissue to produce shrinkage and scarring. It is commonly used for smaller bleeding internal haemorrhoids. The product and technique vary, and suitability is not determined by grade alone.

The injection can be uncomfortable, and pain or bleeding afterwards is possible. It may be considered as an alternative in selected people whose medicines make banding less suitable, but it is not automatically safe for everyone taking a blood thinner. Ask about expected benefit, possible repeat sessions and why it fits your particular findings.

Infrared coagulation and the examination used with it

Infrared coagulation applies controlled energy that creates heat in internal haemorrhoidal tissue. The treated area scars and shrinks. It is commonly considered for smaller internal haemorrhoids; effectiveness can be lower with more substantial prolapse, so “suitable up to grade III” is not a guarantee that it is the right option.

An anoscope allows the clinician to see and target the area. Mild discomfort or cramping may occur, and repeat treatment can be necessary. Infrared treatment is not the same as freezing tissue. Cryotherapy and electrical coagulation are different techniques, even though the broad aim of reducing troublesome tissue may sound similar.

Haemorrhoidal artery ligation

Haemorrhoidal artery ligation, often called HAL or HALO, identifies arteries supplying the haemorrhoids and ties them with stitches. A Doppler ultrasound probe is often used to locate the vessels. The related term THD refers to transanal haemorrhoidal dearterialisation. A lifting stitch, or mucopexy, may also be used to address prolapse.

This is an operation with an anaesthetic plan, commonly general or spinal anaesthesia, rather than simply another anaesthetic-free office treatment. Compared with excision it may cause less early pain, but haemorrhoids can recur more often. Ask whether the expected symptom relief, likelihood of another procedure and recovery demands suit you. The method does not remove a substantial external component in the same way as excisional surgery.

Excisional haemorrhoidectomy

Haemorrhoidectomy removes the troublesome tissue. It can be considered for large symptomatic external haemorrhoids, combined internal and external disease, advanced prolapse or internal disease that has not responded to, or is unsuitable for, office treatment. It tends to provide durable relief, with more postoperative discomfort than many less invasive options.

Several techniques and instruments are available. The wound may be left open or closed, depending on the approach. General anaesthesia, a regional technique such as spinal anaesthesia, or an appropriate local/sedation arrangement may be used. A spinal and an epidural are related regional approaches but are not identical procedures. Discuss the planned anaesthetic with the team rather than assuming every operation uses the same one.

Stapled haemorrhoidopexy

Stapled haemorrhoidopexy uses a circular stapling device to remove a ring of tissue higher in the rectum and lift prolapsing internal tissue. It also interrupts part of the blood supply. It does not treat external haemorrhoids in the same way as removing them.

Some studies find less early pain and faster initial recovery than excisional surgery. However, recurrent haemorrhoids or prolapse and the need for further treatment are greater concerns, alongside uncommon serious complications. ASCRS guidance does not routinely recommend it as the first surgical choice. A shorter early recovery should be weighed against longer-term outcomes, not treated as proof that stapling is best for everyone.

Blood thinners and preparation need an agreed plan

Tell the treating team about anticoagulants, antiplatelet medicines, non-prescription painkillers, supplements, allergies and bleeding disorders. Banding can cause delayed bleeding when treated tissue separates, including during the second week. The balance between bleeding risk and the risk of a clot requires an individual decision.

Do not stop warfarin, aspirin or another prescribed blood-thinning medicine yourself. If a change is appropriate, the procedural team and prescriber should agree the timing and restart instructions. Also ask about food and drink restrictions, bowel preparation if required, medicines on the day and transport home. Do not apply the preparation for an anaesthetised operation to every office procedure.

Day surgery still needs a recovery plan

Many operations are performed as day cases. Having an anaesthetic does not automatically mean an overnight admission. Staff assess recovery, pain, bleeding and other practical requirements before discharge; some people need a longer stay.

After general anaesthesia or sedation, follow the hospital’s instructions about collection, supervision, driving, alcohol and activities requiring judgement. Arrange help with children or other caring responsibilities. Have the written medication and bowel-care plan, follow-up arrangements and a number to call if there is a problem. A quick trip home is not the same as being ready for work or normal lifting.

Use a tailored pain plan

Pain after excisional surgery is common and may be particularly noticeable with bowel movements. Your plan might include paracetamol, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicine such as ibuprofen when appropriate, or other prescribed treatment. Suitability depends on the procedure, bleeding risk, kidney or stomach conditions and other medicines. Follow the actual prescription rather than a generic schedule from an article.

An opioid such as oxycodone may be needed for some people, but it can cause constipation, sleepiness and other serious harms. Use it only as prescribed and ask when and how to reduce it. Do not increase the dose because pain is unexpectedly worsening; contact the team so a complication or inadequate plan can be considered. Keep medicines safely away from children.

Lorazepam is not a routine substitute for a painkiller

Ativan is a brand name for lorazepam, a benzodiazepine. It should not be presented as a standard first step for everyone recovering from haemorrhoid surgery or given a universal six-hour schedule. Whether it has any role in your care is a prescribing decision.

Combining a benzodiazepine with an opioid, alcohol or other sedating medicines can cause dangerous sedation and slow breathing. Do not add it yourself. If you already take lorazepam regularly, tell the team and do not suddenly stop it without advice, because withdrawal can be serious. Difficulty breathing or being unusually hard to wake after medicines needs emergency help.

Keep stools comfortable and care for the wound

A prescribed laxative or stool softener may help after surgery, especially when pain or opioid use makes passing stool difficult. Aim for stools that pass without straining; both hard stools and repeated diarrhoea can irritate the area. Ask how to adjust the plan if it causes loose stools or is not helping. Avoid delaying bowel movements out of fear, and do not keep pushing when there is nothing to pass.

A warm plain-water bath or sitz bath may ease discomfort if recommended by your surgical team. There is no need to add salt, perfume or antiseptic products unless specifically instructed. Clean gently and follow the directions for any dressing. Fibre and fluids remain useful, with fluid intake adapted to any medical restrictions. Wound care should match the operation you actually had.

Allow time before returning to heavy activity

Recovery varies widely between banding, artery ligation and excisional surgery. Many people need around two weeks away from work after haemorrhoidectomy, while complete comfort and healing can take longer. Some office treatments allow a much quicker return. The amount of lifting, driving or physical work in your day affects what is realistic.

Build activity gradually and follow instructions about heavy lifting, pulling, strenuous exercise and swimming. Gentle movement is different from heavy exertion. Longer-term activity, comfortable bowel habits and support toward a suitable weight may help general health, but none guarantees that haemorrhoids will never recur. Ask for advice tailored to your work and caregiving responsibilities rather than relying on a promise that all symptoms will disappear in one or two weeks.

Recognise bleeding and infection that need urgent help

Some spotting can occur after treatment, but the expected amount and duration depend on the procedure. Seek prompt advice for bleeding beyond the discharge instructions, worsening anal or abdominal pain, fever, concerning discharge, persistent diarrhoea or a new very painful swelling. Being unable to pass urine needs urgent assessment; do not simply wait overnight for it to resolve.

Heavy or continuing bleeding, faintness, severe pain or becoming very unwell needs urgent medical care. Rare complications include an abscess, which is a collection of pus, and sepsis, a dangerous response to infection. Deep injury or perforation after some procedures can lead to inflammation or infection of the abdominal lining, called peritonitis. These are not ordinary recovery symptoms. Tell the urgent-care team which procedure you had and when.

Later problems and follow-up

Problems can also appear after the early recovery period. These include recurrent haemorrhoids, delayed bleeding, constipation or difficulty passing stool, and narrowing of the anal canal, called stenosis or stricture. Some people notice residual skin tags. Less commonly, control of wind or stool may change. A skin tag alone does not prove that the original haemorrhoids have returned.

Report symptoms that persist, recur or interfere with daily life. The team can check healing, review medicines and bowel habits, and decide whether further treatment is needed. Ask what follow-up is planned, whether there are results to discuss and whom to contact after routine clinic hours. A successful procedure includes a clear route back to care if recovery does not follow the expected course.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Treatment begins with confirming the cause of symptoms and discussing appropriate conservative, office and surgical options. Rectal bleeding may need investigation beyond a diagnosis of piles.

The pain plan, bowel care and warning signs should be agreed before discharge. Less early pain does not necessarily mean less recurrence, and blood-thinning medicines require an individual decision.

How BeMama can help

Prepare a list of your medicines, symptoms and recovery responsibilities to discuss with the treating team. BeMama can help organize questions; it cannot select an operation or prescribe postoperative medicines.

When to seek help

Heavy bleeding, inability to pass urine, severe pain, fever or marked illness after a procedure needs urgent assessment. Do not combine opioid and sedating medicines or change blood thinners without a coordinated prescription plan.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Different procedures address different internal and external findings.
  • Most people can begin with measures that reduce straining and improve bowel habits.
  • Artery ligation and stapled surgery have benefits and recurrence trade-offs.
  • Recovery and pain control need an individual plan; one-week promises are unreliable.
  • Know the warning signs and keep the team’s contact details available.

Frequently asked questions

Do most haemorrhoids need surgery?

No. Many improve with bowel-habit and dietary measures, sometimes with medicines or office treatment. An operation is considered according to symptoms and examination findings.

Do grades I to IV apply to external haemorrhoids?

No. They describe how far internal haemorrhoids prolapse and whether they return. An external lump needs its own assessment.

Is rubber-band ligation always painless?

No. Pressure or aching can occur. Severe pain during or after treatment should be reported, and banding must never be attempted at home.

Is infrared treatment the same as freezing?

No. Infrared coagulation uses heat generated by light. Cryotherapy is a different technique.

Can artery ligation be done like office banding without an anaesthetic?

Do not assume that. HAL or THD is an operation with an anaesthetic plan, commonly general or spinal anaesthesia.

Why might stapled surgery not be the first choice?

It can offer less early discomfort, but recurrence and specific serious complications matter. Current ASCRS guidance does not routinely recommend it as first-line surgery.

Should I stop a blood thinner before treatment?

Only under an agreed plan from the treating team and prescriber. The risk of bleeding must be balanced against the risk of a clot.

Should I take Ativan before trying an opioid painkiller?

No general sequence like that is appropriate. Lorazepam is a benzodiazepine, and combining it with an opioid can dangerously slow breathing. Use only the individually prescribed plan.

Should I put salt in a sitz bath?

Use plain warm water unless your surgical team specifically advises an additive. Salt or scented products can irritate a healing wound.

Which recovery symptoms should not wait?

Heavy bleeding, faintness, severe or worsening pain, fever, inability to pass urine or feeling seriously unwell need urgent advice or emergency care. Breathing difficulty or extreme sedation after medicine is an emergency.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
